title: Byte Order: Little vs Big Endian
oneLiner: The same multi-byte number gets stored in opposite byte order depending on the machine -- and mixing them up is a real, recurring bug.
keyTakeaway: Big-endian stores the most-significant byte (the one holding the largest place values, like the 1 in 1,000) FIRST (left to right, the way you'd write the number by hand). Little-endian stores the least-significant byte first. Almost all consumer hardware (x86, the processor family in most PCs and servers, and ARM, the family in phones, in the mode they normally run) is little-endian; network protocols are traditionally big-endian ("network byte order"), which is exactly why translating between the two shows up constantly at that boundary.
explanation: A single byte has no order to worry about -- endianness only matters once a value takes up MORE than one byte in memory, like a 32-bit integer or float. Take the number 0x12345678: conceptually it's four bytes, 0x12 (most significant) through 0x78 (least significant). Memory is a long row of bytes, each with a numbered position called its address. Big-endian memory stores them in that same reading order: address 0 holds 0x12, address 1 holds 0x34, and so on -- "big end first." Little-endian memory stores them backwards: address 0 holds 0x78 (the LEAST significant byte), address 3 holds 0x12 -- "little end first." Neither is "more correct"; it's a hardware/format convention, and the two are only compatible if whoever reads the bytes back knows which order they were written in. This is the exact bug that broke this app's Floating Point calculator during development: the code wrote a float32's bytes in the browser's native order (little-endian) but read them back assuming big-endian, silently scrambling every value -- a positive number came out reading as negative.
